deep.reconstruction:
The page has no computations. It holds methodological and polemical notes from Hilbert's notebook (Cod. Ms. Hilbert 600), made around 1900-1902 during his quarrel with Felix Klein's applied and model-based programme.

(1) Models and the Kötter reference. Hilbert writes that a model should [n]ie/wie be an end in itself (the reading is uncertain). He refers to Fritz Kötter's polemic against Klein and Sommerfeld (the Theorie des Kreisels) about the purpose of numerical computation.

(2) The 'Latrinen' joke. Hilbert writes: 'Yes, if one could clean latrines by means of the quadratic reciprocity law, as one can by means of the hydraulic formulas.' The sketch shows a pipe with a jet entering a wider channel and a side inlet marked with an arrow, i.e. a jet pump or injector. The annotation reads 'wo hier ein Ansaugen statthat' ('where suction takes place here'). This is an ironic jab at the utilitarian valuation of mathematics.

(3) Heuristic principle. Hilbert writes: 'All thinking consists in finding problems simpler than the given one.' In a sense every problem is a problem of the calculus of variations. One seeks the problem that minimises 'difficulty' among the unsolved problems, subject to the side condition (Nebenbedingung) that its solution is necessary for solving the given problem. Schematically, in my notation: minimise c(Q) over unsolved Q, subject to 'P requires Q'. This is a metaphor, not a theorem.

(4) Worked example. Take the problem of proving the parallel theorem (or possibly Pascal's theorem; see corrections) in the plane without the parallel axiom, or of showing it is unprovable. Hilbert recognises this as equivalent to determining all 3-parameter groups of continuous transformations of the plane, without assuming the transforming functions are differentiable. This is the Helmholtz-Lie space problem with differentiability removed: the plane's motion group is 3-dimensional, and its possible forms correspond to Euclidean, hyperbolic and elliptic geometry. One then sees that one must first determine all 1- and 2-parameter groups. That is the reduction to subgroups such as the 1-parameter rotation group about a fixed point. This is exactly the programme Hilbert carried out in 'Über die Grundlagen der Geometrie' (Math. Ann. 56, 1902; Appendix IV of the Grundlagen der Geometrie). There he characterises plane Euclidean and Bolyai-Lobachevsky geometry through a continuous motion group, without differentiability. The same idea underlies Hilbert's 5th problem (1900).

(5) The final two lines are struck through. They read roughly: 'Theorie der math. Physik erscheint ... Anordnung gerafter(?) ... Gesetze ... alle'.
errors: No mathematical derivation, so no computational errors.

The claimed equivalence is heuristic. A transitive 3-parameter group on the plane does not by itself yield a geometry; Hilbert's 1902 paper needs further axioms (Jordan-curve neighbourhoods, closure of motion sets, rotation behaviour). He is also silent on the third case, elliptic geometry, which his 1902 axioms exclude.
